newsitem.title: USA: Mich. Tribe asks judge to stop Detroit casino.
newsitem.headline: Mich. Tribe asks judge to stop Detroit casino.

text.p: A Michigan Indian tribe Wednesday asked a federal judge to stop the process for awarding Detroit casino licenses until its challenge to the law permitting them has been resolved.
U.S. District Judge Douglas Hillman set a hearing on the tribe's request for Aug. 20 in federal court in Grand Rapids. The lawsuit has been assigned to Judge Robert Bell.

Lac Vieux Desert Band of the Lake Superior Chippewa Indians contended in a February lawsuit that the casino referendum approved last year included unconstitutional preferences for backers of the legislation.
With Friday's deadline for filing initial casino applications approaching, the tribe sought to accelerate the process, spokesman Robert Kolt said.
"The tribe's only intention is to be part of gaming in Detroit," Kolt said. "The tribe just wants a level playing field."
The tribe operates a casino on a 200-acre reservation near the Wisconsin border in Michigan's upper peninsula and also plans to seek a Detroit casino license.

"The ballot referendum, city ordinances and amending state legislation, prohibits our tribe from competing for a casino license on equal terms with other gaming interests," Tribal Chairman John McGeshick said.

Anthony Neely, a spokesman for Detroit Mayor Dennis Archer, said the city will respond to the injunction request and does not expect the lawsuit to affect the schedule for awarding casino development licenses.
The casino referendum included the Atwater Group and Greektown Casino LLC as preferred parties for licensing. Detroit's timeline includes beginning construction in early 1998 on the three casinos.
